claims.claim: Color is a visual perception, the way the eye reads different wavelengths of light, and in UX design it functions as a design language that communicates information, guides behavior, and creates meaningful user experiences.

Color communicates meaning in interfaces through conventions such as red borders for errors and green checkmarks for success, and colors should be used consistently so a color means the same thing everywhere.
Color groups related elements: color-coded categories, tabs, and buttons organize features into manageable visual groups so users can scan an interface without reading every label.
Color creates emphasis: an accent color reserved for what should stand out most, such as the primary call to action, draws the user's attention to the most important element.

On the color wheel, the primary colors are red, yellow, and blue; secondary colors (orange, green, purple) are mixes of two primaries; and tertiary colors are mixes of a primary and a secondary, such as yellow-orange.

Common color schemes include complementary (colors opposite on the wheel, producing high contrast), analogous (colors next to each other, producing low contrast), and monochromatic (tones and shades of a single hue).

There is little real research proving a universal effect of a particular color on emotions; color interpretation varies from culture to culture (for example, red means stop in many Western contexts, and the color of money is red in China but green in the United States), so meaning should not be assumed to travel.

WCAG success criterion 1.4.1 states that color is not used as the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response, or distinguishing a visual element; color coding is acceptable when complemented by another visual indication.
Text and images of text need sufficient light-dark contrast with their background to be readable; WCAG 1.4.3 sets a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for normal text (3:1 for large text).

Roughly eight percent of men and half a percent of women have some form of color vision deficiency, and color appearance varies across devices, lighting, and individual perception, so color choices should be tested with real users including people with different visual abilities.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Popular articles and some marketing material promise universal color meanings (for example, that blue always means trust), while Nielsen Norman Group states that little real research proves a universal emotional effect of a particular color and that interpretation varies by culture. This lesson follows the evidence-based position: color conventions are local and learned, and choices must be tested with real users.

sourceRecords.title: Using Color to Enhance Your Design
sourceRecords.notes: Verified via Wayback Machine snapshot (2026-05-16) because the live page returns HTTP 403 to automated clients; article by Kelley Gordon, June 6, 2021. Supports: the color wheel groups (primary red, yellow, blue; secondary orange, purple, green as mixes of primaries; tertiary colors as mixes of primary and secondary); color harmonies (analogous, complementary, split-complementary, triadic, monochromatic); the claim that little research proves a universal emotional effect of specific colors and that interpretation varies by culture (red for stop, green for go; the color of money differs by country); reserving an accent color for what should stand out, such as the primary call to action; consistent color use across screens; and usability testing for legibility and accessibility. Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Understanding SC 1.4.1 Use of Color (Level A)
sourceRecords.notes: Verified via Wayback Machine snapshot (2026-07-19); the live page returns HTTP 403 to automated clients. Supports success criterion 1.4.1: color is not used as the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response, or distinguishing a visual element; examples include required fields marked only in red and error states shown only in red; color coding is acceptable when complemented by another visual indication; people with color deficiencies, older users with limited color vision, and monochrome displays are the reasons behind the rule. Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Understanding SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) (Level AA)
sourceRecords.notes: Verified via Wayback Machine snapshot (2026-08-18); the live page returns HTTP 403 to automated clients. Supports success criterion 1.4.3: the visual presentation of text and images of text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text), so text can be read by people with moderately low vision or impaired contrast perception; adequate light-dark contrast between text and background is needed for good readability. Used only lightly in this lesson because wcag-basics is a sibling topic that owns the details. Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Color in UX Design
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via HTTP on 2026-08-21 (page updated 2026). Supports: color as a visual perception that functions as a design language communicating information and guiding behavior; color psychology as general guidelines rather than universal rules (in the West, red signals urgency or error, blue conveys trust, green indicates success, yellow draws attention or suggests caution); cultural symbolism varying across cultures (red signals danger in many Western contexts but luck and prosperity in Chinese culture); color-coded categories and tabs organizing features into visual groups; color serving feedback and system status (red borders for errors, green checkmarks for success); color vision deficiency affecting roughly 8% of men and 0.5% of women; and testing color choices with real users across devices and lighting conditions. Facts restated in original prose.
